author: ghodss
title: Root command's Help() doesn't print Usage
body:
As pointed out by @jcelliott in #3, running the root command without any arguments, or running the root command with `<command> help` does not print the Command.Long description.[1] Given that the help command is the only venue in which you can see the Long description, this is a bug. (The README indicates that the Long description should be printed as well.)

The issue is that Command.Usage() doesn't print the Long description, only Command.Help() does. This would be fine if Command.Help() always printed Usage. But instead, Command.Help() only prints Usage if the Command is Runnable, which the root command typically is not. Instead, Command.Help() should print Usage if the command is Runnable OR if the command HasSubCommands.

When Help() is fixed to print Usage in those cases, Help is often the preferred thing to print, not Usage.

I am submitting a PR which fixes the Help() behavior and changes a few Usage() references to use Help() instead.

[1] As an aside, if you `go get` the latest cobra release, this behavior is visible on Hugo right now.

title: Unknown commands '-h' and '--help'
body:
Using the default example with 'Short' & 'Long' added to rootCmd:

```
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "github.com/spf13/cobra"
    "strings"
)

func main() {

    var echoTimes int

    var cmdPrint = &cobra.Command{
        Use:   "print [string to print]",
        Short: "Print anything to the screen",
        Long: `print is for printing anything back to the screen.
        For many years people have printed back to the screen.
        `,
        Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
            fmt.Println("Print: " + strings.Join(args, " "))
        },
    }

    var cmdEcho = &cobra.Command{
        Use:   "echo [string to echo]",
        Short: "Echo anything to the screen",
        Long: `echo is for echoing anything back.
        Echo works a lot like print, except it has a child command.
        `,
        Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
            fmt.Println("Print: " + strings.Join(args, " "))
        },
    }

    var cmdTimes = &cobra.Command{
        Use:   "times [# times] [string to echo]",
        Short: "Echo anything to the screen more times",
        Long: `echo things multiple times back to the user by providing
        a count and a string.`,
        Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
            for i := 0; i < echoTimes; i++ {
                fmt.Println("Echo: " + strings.Join(args, " "))
            }
        },
    }

    cmdTimes.Flags().IntVarP(&echoTimes, "times", "t", 1, "times to echo the input")

    var rootCmd = &cobra.Command{
        Use:   "usage string",
        Short: "short string",
        Long:  "long string",
    }

    rootCmd.AddCommand(cmdPrint, cmdEcho)
    cmdEcho.AddCommand(cmdTimes)
    rootCmd.Execute()
}
```

author: bep
title: Expose annotations in the Cobra API
body:
Ref. the bashcompletion sample:

```
 annotations := []string{"json", "yaml", "yml"}
    annotation := make(map[string][]string)
    annotation[cobra.BashCompFilenameExt] = annotations

    flag := &pflag.Flag{
        Name:        "filename",
        Shorthand:   "f",
        Usage:       usage,
        Value:       value,
        DefValue:    value.String(),
        Annotations: annotation,
    }
    cmd.Flags().AddFlag(flag)
```

There are a couple of issues with this:

2) It's kind of missing the point of `Cobra` being the abstraction it is.

author: mwmahlberg
title: Generated output should be done with cobra command line tool
body:
Currently, man pages / Markdown documentation / bash completion are generated when the respective command is called.

This is problematic. Let's take Linux for example. When a man page is generated, it might well not be generated by a user allowed to put it into the correct location. So the proper location can not be used for the path parameter of `GenManTree`. On the other hand, man pages should not be distributed over the file system.

Doing the generation via a special command does not prevent that, and would clutter the program with a command used only during installation.

It would be better to at least have an option to have man pages / Markdown / bash completion generated by the `cobra` command line tool.

An API change is maybe a hard sell, but what about a `Command.ExecuteC` or something?

author: algrebe
title: Pre Run and Post Run chain functions
body:
W.r.t https://github.com/spf13/cobra/issues/216

Persitent\* functions execute only if the child has not overridden the parent.

Consider the following scenario:
Root command has a PersistentPreRun in which it defines a logger, sets the log level and starts a profiler.
Root command has a PersistentPostRun function in which it stops the profiler safely, closes file descriptors etc, whatever is needed for a clean and safe exit.

Child command also has a PersistentPreRun and PersistentPostRun for its own reasons - for its own child commands.
Since the child command has defined its own Persistent_, the root command Persistent_ are not called. 

To solve this, there need to be hooks that get fired irrespective of the child having its own hook - these are chain hooks.

PreRunChain gets called in the order of parent to child

PostRunChain gets called in the order of child to parent
i.e. root PreRunChain -> child PreRunChain

And PostRunChain gets called in the order of child to parent
i.e. child PostRunChain -> root PostRunChain

So for the previous scenario

root PreRunChain sets logger and profiler
child PreRunChain does its own initialization etc

```
/* the usual stuff that existed before - the overriding logic
PersistentPreRun
PreRun
Run
PostRun
PersistentPostRun
*/
```

child PostRunChain frees up its own things, for its safe exit
root PostRunChain stops the profiler


would parse `path/to/config.json` for commands and execute `server` in case it is present and properly configured.

Any ideas or hints are highly appreciated.

author: onlyjob
title: Use semantic versioning
body:
Please consider assigning version numbers and tagging releases. Tags/releases
are useful for downstream package maintainers (in [Debian](http://debian.org) and other distributions) to export source tarballs, automatically track new releases and to declare dependencies between packages. Read more in the [Debian Upstream Guide](https://wiki.debian.org/UpstreamGuide#Releases_and_Versions).

Versioning provides additional benefits to encourage vendoring of a particular (e.g. latest stable) release contrary to random unreleased snapshots.

Thank you.

See also
- http://semver.org/
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_versioning

author: MarkDBlackwell
title: README misleadingly states any filesystem organization is allowed
body:
[README.md](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blame/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/README.md#L142) says "[Y]ou are welcome to provide your own organization[.]" A diagram of a "typical" filesystem tree follows. It includes `appName/cmd/`.

However, rather than fully allow "your own organization," the current code ([cobra/cmd/helpers.go](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/cobra/cmd/helpers.go#L41)) apparently looks only in certain directories immediately under the project root: `cmd/`, `cmds/`, `command/` and `commands/`.

Should `README.md` be supplemented by language like, "as long as you assign your command directory one of the following names: `cmd/`, `cmds/`, `command/` or `commands/`"?

That would facilitate understanding IMO by new users, and help the growth of Cobra.

author: MarkDBlackwell
title: Cobra disagrees with archetypal example Hugo
body:
Arguably, the archetypal example of a Cobra user is [Hugo](https://github.com/spf13/hugo). However, Hugo apparently doesn't match what Cobra currently generates for new projects (`{{appName}}/cmd/`). Instead, it contains the directory, [`hugo/commands/`](https://github.com/spf13/hugo/tree/f914774f6bcb2416004101112c0f2dd1cd664176/commands).

Which directory name for commands is the least confusing way to go? Is it:
1. What Cobra generates: `cmd/`? or
2. Hugo's usage: `commands/`?

Both work. Yet the difference seems needlessly confusing for new Cobra adopters. They likely will be experimenting with both Hugo and Cobra (as well as browsing the source of both) while learning Cobra.

Aligning both Cobra and Hugo to use the same directory name for commands (insofar as possible) would make such learning easier, and IMO help the growth of Cobra.

BTW, IMO the easiest name to learn is `commands/`.

author: MarkDBlackwell
title: Cobra 'init' should error out, if user specifies unknown license
body:
The README says:

> The `cobra init` command...will also automatically apply the [license](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blame/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/README.md#L186) you specify to your application.
> An example `~/.cobra.yaml` file:
> [license](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blame/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/README.md#L240): MIT

This doesn't tell us what strings we can use, in order to select the license we want.

I tried the following in my configuration file:

``` bash
$ cat ~/.cobra.yml
author: {{My name and email}}
license: Simplified BSD license
```

This seemed reasonable (to me; I am a new user of Go and Cobra). Note that I copied the string "Simplified BSD license" directly [from the Cobra source](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/cobra/cmd/licenses.go#L382), where it was labeled (in struct key `Name`) as the name of the desired license.

Anyway, the result was:
1. "Licensed under the Apache License" (in the header); and
2. "Apache License" (in the LICENSE file).

So, apparently Cobra chose the default, despite my attempt to specify a  license. Plus, it did so without warning.

Whenever the user attempts to specify a license, and Cobra can't determine what it is, IMO Cobra should error out.

This would be far better than Cobra proceeding IMO with a wrong license (even if it were to print a warning). The fact that it proceeds anyway increases slightly IMO users' overall difficulty of later recovery.

Instead, when a user's license specification is erroneous, Cobra should help the user IMO by printing out a list of valid license specifying strings.

author: MarkDBlackwell
title: Phrase 'go path bin' unclear in README
body:
README section [Using the Cobra Generator](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blame/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/README.md#L179) says:

> This will create the cobra executable under your go path bin directory!

Relatively new Go users might confuse this with their `$PATH`s directory of Go executables (`C:\Go\bin` for Windows, or `/usr/local/go/bin`). So IMO this should be:

> This will create the cobra executable under your `$GOPATH` `bin` directory!

or:

> This will create the cobra executable under your `$GOPATH/bin` directory!

author: MarkDBlackwell
title: docs: "Commands" should be called subcommands
body:
README section [Overview](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blame/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/README.md#L38) says:

> Cobra provides:
> Easy subcommand-based CLIs: app server, app fetch, etc.

However, instead, elsewhere in the README (and also in its source, I suppose), Cobra calls `{{App}} server` and `{{App}} fetch` "commands."

For an example of this, README section [Concepts](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blame/7c674d9e72017ed25f6d2b5e497a1368086b6a6f/README.md#L65) says:

> Cobra is built on a structure of commands, arguments & flags.
> **Commands** represent actions, **Args** are things and **Flags** are modifiers for those actions.

This conflicts with general Unix usage, which (e.g.) calls `git checkout mybranch` a "command" and (within it)`checkout` an "argument." Cobra's usage here IMO is less clear (as well as inconsistent with its README reference above to "subcommands").

Calling them "subcommands" IMO seems clearest for new users (as well as helping them by maintaining consistency with Unix).

Therefore, `server`, `fetch`, etc. IMO should be called "subcommands" (or "AppCommands") throughout the documentation, to help new users and others.

author: knz
title: Man page generator generates inconsistent file names and SEE ALSO references
body:
We encountered this in CockroachDB (xref https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/4917)
- `GenManTree` in `doc/man_docs.go` forces the command separator to be `"_"`, which causes `GenManTreeFromOpts` to generate file names for man pages to be `like_this.1`
- Meanwhile, `genMan` replaces spaces in names by `"-"` always.

As a result, when the reader reads the "SEE ALSO" section she might see a reference to `this-command(1)` whereas the command she has to type to read that man page is actually `man this_command`.

May I suggest to use dashes always, that is, set the options in `GenManTree` to use `"-"`.

author: kofalt
title: Documenting a positional argument and suppressing `[flags]` when appropriate
body:
The readme references an example command that has a positional argument:
```
git clone URL --bare
```
To document that in Hugo, here's what I would start with:
```go
cloneCmd := &cobra.Command{
	Use:   "clone",
	Short: "Clone a repository into a new directory",
	Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
		// stub
	},
}
```
Which produces:
```
$ example clone --help
Clone a repository into a new directory

Usage:
  example clone [flags]
```

This stub could use a few improvements:

1. The positional parameter `URL` is not specified in the help.
1. I'd have to manually check the `args` array for `URL`, invent some error messages, etc.
1. The documentation specifies `[flags]`, but there are no flags!

Any ideas on how I could tackle these improvements?

The first one could probably be fixed by setting `Use` to `"clone [URL]"`, but the third one is the real pickle. As far as I can tell I'd have to copy and modify [the default template](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/92ea23a837e66f46ac9e7d04fa826602b7b0a42d/command.go#L339-L363), at which point I'm detached from the official version and I'd have to maintain my "fork" of the template, which I'd rather avoid.

body:
I have two level deep subcommand structure. I have "backends" for which I need to load configuration before any second-level subcommands run, but the first-level subcommands are only showing help, in which case I don't want to load configuration because these can be extremely expensive (e.g. coming from a database or network). So I would like to show only the help when running a first-level subcommand, but I need to load the configuration when a second-level sub command is run, because without it, I can't run the second-level subcommands.
Currently, this is not possible in Cobra because `cobra.OnInitialize` will always run before any command, `PersistentPreRun` hook will always run before the second-level subcommand and `PersistentPostRun` hook will always run too late.
I was thinking about setting a boolean `dontLoadConfiguration` somewhere when running first-level subcommands (when showing only help), but there is not a point I could check that either.

Coming from Python, with the use of the great Click framework, [it's possible to determine in the main command if a sub command is going to be executed](http://click.pocoo.org/5/api/#click.Context.invoked_subcommand) with the `Context.invoked_subcommand` boolean. This would be nice for Cobra too.

Okay, I lied a little bit :) because setting the same `loadConfiguration` function in *every single* subcommand of the library (I have dozens) is possible in the `PreRun` hooks in the second-level subcommands, but it's really tedious. Ideally, I would like to set it once in the `rootCmd` and forget it and happily develop new subcommands without forgetting to set `loadConfiguration` once again...

author: Fjolnir-Dvorak
title: Long description formatting
body:
The long description formatting is handling line breaks in the IDE as a new Line. Also Tab characters are not removed at the beginning of the line.

**Example:**
```
var (
	GameCMD = &cobra.Command{
		Use:   "game",
		Short: "Utilities modifying the game data.",
		Long: `This package interacts directly with the game files
			or wil generate and deploy them. To archive that it looks
			for the location of the game files inside the windows registry.`,
	}
)
```

The example above uses tab characters for indentation (it is the default behaviour of the IDE and "go fmt" is not replacing it with whitespaces which leads to a valid code design pattern.) and new-lines to make it human-readable (line length, and "abc" + "def" + "ghi" is quite ugly).

**My suggestion:**
1. Minify the long description (deleting all tabs, newlines and double spaces).
2. parse '\n' to a "by the user forced" newline
3. Soft wrap the whole text and indent it as needed.

author: bvk
title: Using cobra.Command for web browser based CLI interfaces
body:
Hi,


I have the following use-case: I want to run a Golang daemon that can
be interacted with a CLI interface from shell and also from web
browsers.

I can use Cobra package for implementing command-line processing for
normal shells. I would like to use the same modules, code and logic
for also processing CLI commands from web browsers.

For example, josh.js package (See
http://sdether.github.io/josh.js/index.html) provides a shell-like
interface for web browsers. It can be used to parse user input into
os.Args like arguments.

My plan is to make the client side javascript send os.Args-like
arguments to the Golang daemon in a POST request and let the Golang
daemon use the same cobra.Command modules to process and execute the
command-line and return the output in a POST response.

This allows me to export all CLI features (like, help, etc.) to the
web interface. Also, I need to implement CLI processing only once.

QUESTIONS

1. In execution of a shell CLI program, Command.Execute happens only
once and program exits afterwards. With the above mentioned web CLI
interface, Command.Execute should happen on the daemon in the context
of a single POST request. Daemon should continue to run and process
next CLI request. Is this behavior feasible by cobra package?

2. Normally cobra.Command objects are declared at global scope and
only one instance of a cobra.Command object exists for each
subcommand. With the web CLI interface, multiple POST requests can be
executing multiple commands in parallel in the daemon. Executing
multiple cobra.Command objects in parallel requires them to be
thread-safe and don't use or update any the shared state. So, are
executions of multiple instances of a cobra.Command safe?


Can someone knowledgeable with cobra package internals shed some light
on how to achieve my use-case or if it is even feasible with current cobra
package implementation?


Thanks,
Chaitanya

author: zevdg
title: cobra/doc has some problems with dep (blackfriday major version change)
body:
The root cause of the problem is cpuguy83/go-md2man#28

The owner of blackfriday kindly left the master branch of the repo on the v1 API so it wouldn't break go get.  However, dep tries to do the actual right thing and defaults by grabbing the latest tagged release (v2.0) instead of whatever is on the master branch unless there is a constraint somewhere that tells it not to.  Since go-md2man doesn't support the 2.0 api yet, this causes breakage.  I'm able to add a constraint in my own project to fix it, but obviously, we don't want every app to have to add this constraint.  Ideally, the root issue above should be the place to fix this, but a constraint could be added here until the issue is resolved upstream.

author: nnutter
title: Question about using command's config file for subcommands
body:
I'm new to Go and to Cobra/Viper so it's likely I'm trying to do something overly complicated and I'm not seeing much documentation about integrating Cobra subcommands with a command's config file.  I am creating a command with sub-commands and would like to support pulling flag values from Viper so that there is basically a hierarchical lookup from command line to a subsection in config file to flag default.

In a command file I can have an `init()` like,

```go
func init() {
	subCmd1.AddCommand(subCmd2)

	subCmd2.Flags().String("flag1", "my default", "my usage")
	viper.BindPFlag("subCmd1.SubCmd2.flag1", subCmd2.Flags().Lookup("flag1"))
}
```

But what I think I want is to be able to `BindPFlags` but to a sub-tree of the config,

```go
func init() {
	subCmd1.AddCommand(subCmd2)

	subCmd2.Flags().String("flag1", "my default", "my usage")

	viper.BindPFlags(subCmd2.Flags(), "subCmd1.subCmd2")
}
```

So in `Run()` when I do `viper.GetString("flag1")` it would essentially be the same as `viper.GetString("subCmd1.SubCmd2.flag1")`.

The motivation being to avoid having to call `viper.BindPFlag()` _n_ times which I assume is also the motivations for `viper.BindPFlags()`.

Is there a way to do this already or, maybe, a recommended alternative?

author: burdiyan
title: Init does not work with a GOPATH with multiple workspaces
body:
$GOPATH environmental variable can specify multiple workspace, as $PATH can. For example `GOPATH=/code/foo:/code/bar`. More on that in this post: https://dmitri.shuralyov.com/blog/18

In this case, when you do `go get github.com/spf13/cobra` in will be installed in the first workspace. Then when you run `cobra init baz` inside a directory in the second workspace, Cobra will fail with: `Error: Cobra only supports project within $GOPATH` and that directory `baz` will be created with LICENSE file only.

Desired behaviour: `cobra init` should be able to create projects inside any part of the $GOPATH.

Notice the extra space at the end. Either the `=` should be removed or the trailing space.

author: nak3
title: RFE: Support OnlySubCommands arg validation to make subcommand get suggestions
body:
### Motivation

Currently, suggestions for "unknown command" are not working for
**sub**commands. For example code[1](wants to accept only when 
subcommand specified), I expected that cobra give us suggestions like:

_Expected_
~~~
  $ go run main.go echo time
  Error: unknown command "time" for "echo"

  Did you mean this?
   	times
~~~

However, cobra does not suggest anything unfortunately.
`SuggestFor:` attribute also does not work currently.

### Workaround

If I use `OnlyValidArgs` for the subcommands, this could be
solve. However, it does not suit when a command has many subcommands 
and makes it makes difficult to maintain.

### Proposal patch

https://github.com/spf13/cobra/pull/635

[1] example code
~~~
package main

import (
        "fmt"
        "strings"

        "github.com/spf13/cobra"
)

func main() {
        var echoTimes int
        var cmdEcho = &cobra.Command{
                Use:   "echo",
                Short: "My root command",
                Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
                        fmt.Println("Don't want to call this...")
                },
        }

        var cmdTimes = &cobra.Command{
                Use: "times [# times] [string to echo]",
                Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
                        for i := 0; i < echoTimes; i++ {
                                fmt.Println("Echo: " + strings.Join(args, " "))
                        }
                },
        }
        cmdTimes.Flags().IntVarP(&echoTimes, "times", "t", 1, "times to echo the input")
        var rootCmd = &cobra.Command{Use: "echo"}
        rootCmd.AddCommand(cmdEcho)
        cmdEcho.AddCommand(cmdTimes)
        rootCmd.Execute()
}
~~~

author: integrii
title: Consider changing `cmd/` directory as cobra command recommendation
body:
Hello @spf13 and thank you for your many great contributions.  I contributed to Hugo some time ago and use it for several sites!

The typical go pattern is to use the `cmd` directory like an index of all buildable binaries in a project.  Cobra directly conflicts with this by recommending that the `cmd` directory is used to hold small packages which each contain cobra command packages.

Please consider recommending a more compatible file structure, such as this one that nests cobra commands with their relevant binaries:

```
project/
    Dockerfile
    kubernetes.yaml
    README.md
    cmd/
        binaryNameA/
            main.go
            cobraCommandA/
                cobraCommandA.go
            cobraCommandB/
                cobraCommandB.go
        binaryNameB/
            main.go
            otherStuff.go
    pkg/
        packageName/
            packageName.go
```

Or perhaps this layout, which organizes the cobra command packages as packages:

```
project/
    Dockerfile
    kubernetes.yaml
    README.md
    cmd/
        binaryNameA/
            main.go
        binaryNameB/
            main.go
            otherStuff.go
    pkg/
        packageName/
            packageName.go
        cobraCommandA/
            cobraCommandA.go
        cobraCommandB/
            cobraCommandB.go
```

The goal here is to enable the typical `cmd/` directory behavior - rather than trying to make cobra users decide which layout to use.

Thanks again!

author: itskingori
title: Idea: support repeated flags to allow lists
body:
Borrowing from [this SO example][1] using the built-in `flag` library, it's possible to do something like this:

```go
package main

import "flag"

type arrayFlags []string

func (i *arrayFlags) String() string {
    return "my string representation"
}

func (i *arrayFlags) Set(value string) error {
    *i = append(*i, value)
    return nil
}

var myFlags arrayFlags

func main() {
    flag.Var(&myFlags, "list1", "Some description for this param.")
    flag.Parse()
}
```

Such that it is possible to do this:

```bash
go run your_file.go --list1 value1 --list1 value2
```

And get an slice of strings in the `list1` flag. I've checked issues and documentation and it seems that this is not possible via cobra. Feel free to correct me if I'm wrong. If not, I'd like propose that this feature be considered.

Ps: I've tried repeated flags and the value of the last flag is picked up. Previous ones are somewhat discarded.

Ps 2: Obviously, you can use a comma-delimited list and split on the comma. Just figured I'd throw the idea out there. This is not a blocker, so don't feel obliged in any way.

[1]: https://stackoverflow.com/a/28323276/2184155

author: pbnj
title: Add Support for Plugins
body:
Hi,

I apologize in advance if this has been previously requested. A cursory search did not yield related issues.

I would love to see a plugin-based architecture support in Cobra.

Some Go apps/CLIs have achieved this plugin-based architecture using [`go-plugin`](https://github.com/hashicorp/go-plugin) library (e.g. Hashicorp's Terraform, Nomad, Packer). `go-plugin` itself achieves this via gRPC contract between host and child processes. Other Go apps have achieved similar plugin-based architecture by executing external binaries that satisfy a JSON contract (e.g. [Buffalo](https://github.com/gobuffalo/buffalo/blob/master/plugins/plugins.go)).

Heroku's Node.js [Open CLI Framework](https://oclif.io/docs/plugins.html) supports [plugins](https://oclif.io/docs/plugins.html).

It would be nice to have plugin support in our beloved CLI library/framework.

Based on consensus from the Cobra maintainers & contributors on this feature request, I could also try to tackle this challenge. 

I'm curious what/how everyone else feels about this?

Thank you.

author: Shamus03
title: Multiple commands' custom completion functions collide
body:
## The issue

Custom completions use a function named `__custom_func`, which does not change between commands.  Each cobra utility defines a `__custom_func` for its own use, but these multiple commands all overwrite the same function.

## Expected behavior

Multiple cobra utilities' `__custom_func` definitions should not collide/overwrite each other.

## Steps to reproduce

Create two cobra utilities with separate `__custom_func` definitions as described [here](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/master/bash_completions.md).  Generate their bash completion scripts and place them in the proper location.  Reload your shell and type `type __custom_func` to get the definition, and notice that one of the commands' completions will not work.  Removing one of the bash completion scripts will ensure the other one works, and vice-versa.

## Suggested solution

In `__handle_reply`, before `__custom_func` is evaluated, the script should search for a function named `__custom_func_COMMAND` where COMMAND is the name of the root command (making it somewhat unique) and evaluate that if it exists.  To ensure backwards compatibility, `__custom_func` should be run if no matching function is defined.

## Proposal

I think there is a good opportunity to improve the `add` command by making the generated go file templatized which makes helps repeatedly written code be standardized.

## Feature

* Enable Developer to use preferred file name.
* Enable Developer to use preferred generated code.

author: Fjolnir-Dvorak
title: Feature request: Interactive mode for the generator
body:
This feature request ist based on the commend from anthonyfok in [pull/485](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/pull/485#issuecomment-419209935).

The Idea is to add an interactive mode for the cobra generator to make people more aware of the decisions they can make and why they should care. One example for that would be the standard config directory and/or -file which should be used for the application. In an linux environment there are different standards for where the config should lie and the developer should decide which to use.
Another bonus would be that the generator could me made more complicated and feature ritch without making it more difficult to use.

One big problem that comes up with this change is that is slows down the pace with which an application is generated. To accomodate for this issue there are several possibilities:
- create a local configuration file for the project containing all the informations on how the project was generated and with which version of cobra on project initialization and modification.
- Add a flag or an interactive option to save the current generation scheme as default and save that setting into the global cobra config file.

References for good code generators / interactive CLI-Applications already out there:
- [JHipster](https://github.com/jhipster/generator-jhipster)

author: stanislavkozlovski
title: Throw error on em/en dash
body:
en (–) and em (—) dashes are unicode characters which look awfully similar to a hyphen.
http://www.thepunctuationguide.com/hyphen-and-dashes.html

At my company, we've had long debugging sessions examining why our application didn't work the way we intended it to. It turned out that it all came from the initial CLI command, where we use `cobra`.
The current behavior is that an argument with given an em dash (e.g `—-arg`) is totally ignored. We also think that the rest of the string is ignored too (e.g `—-arg --something` - something doesn't get passed either).

Could the library throw an error or at least provide a warning such that we can catch problems like these easily? These dashes are not easily recognizable, especially in a terminal. They're very easy to accidentally copy from somewhere and aren't always obvious.

PS: I can volunteer to fix this if you believe it's the right approach

author: weavejester
title: Support for subcommands separated by a colon
body:
It would be nice if there was a switch to allow subcommands in the `app parent:child` form, rather than `app parent child`. Heroku has made [an argument for using the latter syntax](https://medium.com/@jdxcode/12-factor-cli-apps-dd3c227a0e46#58d3).

Any insight on how to best implement/hack this behavior in Cobra as it stands would also be very much appreciated.

author: koiuo
title: Command.SetErrOutput(io.Writer) for more finegrained testing
body:
> Initially I commented on #607 , but I then found out, that I can't reopen it, hence I decided to create a dedicated issue. I apologize if that's an unwanted noise.

Right now `Command` offers `SetOutput` method to set alternative `io.Writer` implementation for testing stdout/stderr interaction.

I think it would be great to be able to distinct standard output and error output here.

It is not uncommong for commands to report warnings to stderr. For example, take GNU's `ls`

```
$ ls -l /does/not/exist /tmp
ls: cannot access '/does/not/exist': No such file or directory
/tmp:
total 27776
...
```

If I were to reimplement this in go, I'd want to be sure, that `ls: cannot access ...` won't get to stdout, as it may be piped further. So I'd like to have test for that. With current _cobra_ code it is not possible to test this behavior.

It looks like a very straightforward and simple change and we can even make it backward compatible with current API.

If there's interest and/or maintainers are open for this change, I'd be willing to work on it.

author: llonchj
title: Command hierarchy middleware
body:
I have the following command hierarchy: 

```
rootCmd (meant to initialize logging)
+--subCmd (meant to initialize a external service i.e. Redis)
   +--subSubCmd (meant to perform an action)
```

I would like the execution of subSubCmd to run a middleware pattern to setup and teardown each inheritance level.

The current PersistentPreRun and PersistentPostRun does something similar but [stops at the first command with the function](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/master/command.go#L744) and also interates from parent.

Is there an existing mechanism in cobra to do that? If not, do you think it will be an interesting feature?

author: albertyw
title: bash_completion code should quote variables
body:
The bash code template in https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/master/bash_completions.go contains a lot of unquoted variables which will cause many errors for people with spaces in their env variables.  A particular case I ran into was a person with a space character in their $PATH which caused a `/bin/bash: line 0: test: -ge: unary operator expected` error.  

Quoting variables is also recommended in bash style guide like [Google's](https://google.github.io/styleguide/shell.xml?showone=Variable_expansion#Variable_expansion).

author: FredrikFolkesson
title: Connecting a StringToString parameter with viper does not seem work.
body:
Hi.

I am trying to connect a `map[string]string` parameter to Viper and it does not seem to work.

In my `init` function I do

```
cmd.PersistentFlags().StringToString("headers", nil, "Headers to use when connecting..")
viper.BindPFlag("headers", cmd.PersistentFlags().Lookup("headers"))
```

and then in the `cmd` function I do
```
headersMap := viper.GetStringMapString("headers")
//use the headers
```

The problem seems to be that what is "saved" in Cobra for the value `headers` is something of the type `StringToString` and not `map[string]string` as I would have thought.
(that is the value of the type I get if I do `cmd.Flag("headers").Value.Type()`

If I save my parameter value by directly specifying the map like this:

```
cmd.PersistentFlags().StringToStringVar(&headersMap, "headers", nil, "Headers to use when connecting ")
```
It correctly saves the value in the map. But then I would have to check that the map is not empty and if it is save the value from viper in the map.


I don't know If this is a bug or If I am missing something?

Thanks!

author: multimeric
title: Generate a toctree in ReST
body:
For most people using the [ReST generator](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/master/doc/rest_docs.md), they will be ultimately building their documentation with [Sphinx](http://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/1.5/index.html). However, ideally Sphinx wants all documents included using a [`toctree` directive](http://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/1.5/markup/toctree.html). For example:

```rest
.. toctree::
   :maxdepth: 2

   intro
   strings
   datatypes
   numeric
```

However, what cobra generates is an index file that looks more like:
```
* `singularity apps <singularity_apps>` 	 - apps <image path>
* `singularity build <singularity_build>` 	 - Build a new Singularity container
* `singularity capability <singularity_capability>` 	 - Manage Linux capabilities on containers
* `singularity exec <singularity_exec>` 	 - Execute a command within container
* `singularity inspect <singularity_inspect>` 	 - Display metadata for container if available
* `singularity instance <singularity_instance>` 	 - Manage containers running in the background
* `singularity keys <singularity_keys>` 	 - Manage OpenPGP key stores
* `singularity oci <singularity_oci>` 	 - Manage OCI containers
```

This works (once you add the `linkHandler` tweak mentioned [here](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/master/doc/rest_docs.md#customize-the-output)), but because it's not part of the toctree, it won't appear in the sidebar or any tables of contents.

As far as I can tell, there's no way to get Cobra to generate a toctree as above, which is an issue because it means I will have to manually create one, and keep it up to date with the CLI, instead of having Cobra build it automatically. 

Is this possible? If not, should toctree generation be an option in `GenReSTTreeCustom`?

author: eine
title: Feature request: support MatchValid(PositionalArgs) OR MinimumValidNArgs, MaximumValidNArgs, RangeValidArgs
body:
For consistency, I think it would be useful to have `MinimumValidNArgs(int)`, `MaximumValidNArgs(int)` and `RangeValidArgs(min, max)` added to the list of supported `Args` formats. The complete list would then be:

- NoArgs
- ArbitraryArgs
- OnlyValidArgs
- MinimumNArgs(int)
- +**MinimumValidNArgs(int)**
- MaximumNArgs(int)
- +**MaximumValidNArgs(int)**
- ExactArgs(int)
- ExactValidArgs(int)
- RangeArgs(min, max)
- +**RangeValidArgs(min, max)**

This is because AFAIK it is not possible ATM to combine e.g. `MinimumNArgs(1)` with `OnlyValidArgs`.

---

An alternative solution is to provide a built-in function such as `matchAll` by @Antolius in [#745](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/issues/745#issuecomment-441326468). For example:

``` go
func MatchValid(p cobra.PositionalArgs) cobra.PositionalArgs {
	return func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
		if err := cobra.OnlyValidArgs(cmd, args); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := p(cmd, args); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	}
}
```

which would allow the following expressions:

- `Args: cobra.MatchValid(cobra.MinimumNArgs(1)), ValidArgs: []string{...}`
- `Args: cobra.MatchValid(cobra.MaximumNArgs(5)), ValidArgs: []string{...}`
- `Args: cobra.MatchValid(cobra.RangeArgs(1, 5)), ValidArgs: []string{...}`
- `Args: cobra.MatchValid(cobra.ArbitraryArgs), ValidArgs: []string{...}`
- `Args: cobra.MatchValid(cobra.ExactArgs(1)), ValidArgs: []string{...}`

Certainly, `MatchValid` can be used implicitly when `ValidArgs` is defined, so the user is not required to type it. Therefore, `OnlyValidArgs` and `ExactValidArgs` can be deprecated from the public API. The list of formats would be:

- NoArgs
- ArbitraryArgs
- MinimumNArgs(int)
- MaximumNArgs(int)
- ExactArgs(int)
- RangeArgs(min, max)

author: vsoch
title: --help doesn't duplicate help
body:
I think I've run into a bug where `--help` with the main executable should print the same thing as `help`, but it does not. Here is an example:

This first example works as expected

```bash
$ container-diff help
container-diff is a CLI tool for analyzing and comparing container images.

Images can be specified from either a local Docker daemon, or from a remote registry.
To specify a local image, prefix the image ID with 'daemon://', e.g. 'daemon://gcr.io/foo/bar'.
To specify a remote image, prefix the image ID with 'remote://', e.g. 'remote://gcr.io/foo/bar'.
If no prefix is specified, the local daemon will be checked first.

Tarballs can also be specified by simply providing the path to the .tar, .tar.gz, or .tgz file.

Usage:
  container-diff [command]

Available Commands:
  analyze     Analyzes an image: [image]
  diff        Compare two images: [image1] [image2]
  help        Help about any command
  version     Print the version of container-diff

Flags:
      --format string      Format to output diff in.
  -h, --help               help for container-diff
  -v, --verbosity string   This flag controls the verbosity of container-diff. (default "warning")

Use "container-diff [command] --help" for more information about a command.
```

This second does not:

```bash
$ container-diff --help
Usage of container-diff:
```
The help is truncated, or is it that we haven't defined what the command should output? I've reported the issue here https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/container-diff/issues/306, and any help/advice to fix up would be greatly appreciated.

author: lorenzoaiello
title: Global command authentication and disabling on certain commands
body:
**Background**
I have an CLI using Cobra that interfaces with APIs that require authentication. There is a "login" command I've added that will generate the appropriate authentication tokens for other requests. If the last generated token has expired, I am preemptively requiring the user log in again.

**Problem**
As the CLI use cases are growing, there is a growing delta of commands that do and do not require authentication. At the moment, the authentication checks are handled in the root `PersistentPreRun` func and there is a hard-coded list of commands that are "exempt" from the authentication checks.

**Ask**
I'm interested in learning if others have experienced a similar issue or might have any recommendations on how best to resolve this.

**Initial Solutions**
I've come up with a couple of alternative solutions that I'm happy to handle the PR work for if they are the direction that the community agrees on.

- Extend `cobra.Command` to allow multiple hooks per command
- Extend `cobra.Command` to include the ability to add additional global elements that could be used for multiple purposes (not just authentication flags)

author: weibeld
title: Bash completion duplicated flags with and without equals signs
body:
I have three flags for a sub-command, two of which are required.

At the beginning, everything looks ok (I think it's a design choice that only the required flags are completed, but not the optional ones):

```bash
$ cmd sub --[tab][tab]
--a-required=    --b-required=
```

But when I fill in one flag and then continue completing, it looks like this:

```bash
$ cmd sub --a-required=foo --[tab][tab]
--a-required    --b-required    --c-optional
--a-required=   --b-required=   --c-optional=
```

So, when there is already one flag on the command line, the behaviour is like this:

1. The optional flag is suggested too
2. Each flag is suggested in a version with and without an equals sign

Here is an example: https://asciinema.org/a/E6ozfI3nfZlZaiEMx4zpJArq5

Furthermore, this only happens when the flag already on the command line has a `=` between the flag name and the value. If flag name and value are separated by a space instead of a `=`, then the behaviour is as expected:

```bash
$ cmd sub --a-required foo --[tab][tab]
--a-required=    --b-required=
```

author: anentropic
title: Docs needed: how best to handle errors in Run
body:
Reading the documentation on the front page, it is not clear to me what the best practice for raising errors from a command's `Run` func is?

Looking at usage of cobra in other projects, the way seems to be just to return `os.Exit(1)` from the body of the `Run` func. I'm a total Go noob so my instinct is probably wrong, but this didn't feel quite 'right' to me. Wouldn't that bypass any `PostRun` hooks? They feel like lifecycle events that should always get a chance to run though.

Then I read to the bottom of issue https://github.com/spf13/cobra/issues/67 and I can see some code got merged four years ago adding a `RunE` hook which returns `error`. (Forgive me if I missed it but it seems this is not mentioned in the docs anywhere? https://github.com/spf13/cobra#prerun-and-postrun-hooks  Are they deprecated?)

This seemed like what I wanted, but the downside is this causes the 'usage' help text to be output. But that's not always appropriate - maybe the user gave perfectly good args to the command but somewhere in the processing of the job an error had to be returned.

So I have gone back to calling `os.Exit` from the body of `Run`.  In the end this is fine for my use case.

All this is just to say it would be good to have the framework's opinion on how to handle errors expressed in the docs somewhere.

author: rck
title: Markdown links broken if sub command calls ResetCommands()
body:
The problem is that the file of the subcommand is generated without the prefix (e.g., as `child.md`), while the `parent.md` links it as `* [parent child](parent_child.md) ...`. This is best demonstrated by this simple example:

```go
package main

import (
        "log"

        "github.com/spf13/cobra"
        "github.com/spf13/cobra/doc"
)

func main() {
        var pb, cb bool
        parent := &cobra.Command{
                Use:   "parent",
                Short: "my main program",
        }
        parent.PersistentFlags().BoolVar(&pb, "parent", false, "parent desc")

        child := &cobra.Command{
                Use:   "child",
                Short: "my subcommand",
                Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
                        err := doc.GenMarkdownTree(parent, "./md")
                        if err != nil {
                                log.Fatal(err)
                        }
                },
        }

        parent.AddCommand(child)
        child.ResetCommands()
        child.Flags().BoolVar(&cb, "child", false, "child desc")

        parent.Execute()
}
```

```sh
$ mkdir md && go run main.go child
$ ls md/
child.md  parent.md
$ tail -n5 md/parent.md
### SEE ALSO

* [parent child](parent_child.md)        - my subcommand

###### Auto generated by spf13/cobra on 23-Aug-2019
```

While this reproducer looks pretty esoteric, the real program uses multiple sub commands that share most persistent flags. With the exception of a few - very distinct - sub commands that just do a `ResetCommands()`.

author: Nuru
title: Please allow booleans to be set false with `no-` prefix
body:
@eparis [wrote](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/issues/613#issuecomment-357706597) 

> Basically, booleans can only take arguments via --bool=[true|false] or for short names -b=[true|false]. You cannot use --bool [true|false] nor can you use the shorthand -b[true|false]

This behavior is unlike any other tool I have encountered. The behavior I am used to and consider "normal" for Unix commands, for boolean options, is:

- For short flags, like `-b`, the option toggles the default value when present. There is generally no way to affirmatively assert the default value with a short flag, though some commands allow it with the same option in the other case, e.g. `-B`
- For long flags, like `--bool`, the named option sets the flag true, and the option with a `no-` prefix sets the flag false, e.g. `--no-bool`. The "usage" for such a flag would be something like

```
-b, --[no-]bool 
```

See, for just one example, [`git-merge`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge). (Truthfully, most commands are written so there is just a default value and a flag which toggles the default, with the flag being prefixed with `no-` when it makes for better style, such as `--no-undefined     Do not allow undefined values`. However, when configuration can come from many sources, a command-line option re-asserting default behavior and overriding the other configuration sources is a valuable feature.) 

The current state where a flag with an argument is written `-f file` but a boolean cannot be written `-b true` is painfully inconsistent as well as awkward, to the point where other options parsers simply do not allow boolean short flags to take arguments. I suggest that instead you automatically create `--bool` and `--no-bool` options for all booleans with long forms and if possible provide some kind of warning against creating a short option that has no effect. 

Note: I have no problem allowing `--bool=false` and I support continuing to allow that as it can make scripting easier. On the other hand, `--no-bool=true` is just plain confusing and should not be allowed.

author: umarcor
title: Maintenance/governance of this project
body:
Earlier this year, in March, I gathered multiple pending PRs with minor/easy fixes/enhancements in a branch I named `trivial`, which was then merged by @eparis. This was almost the only merged contribution since the beginning of the year and until June. @spf13 stepped by, and some long-waiting PRs, such as @jharshman's vgo support, were merged. @spf13 also replied to some other issues, and requested reviews of other users with permissions. During July, @jharshman merged a few fixes, and reviewed some other issues. On August, @bogem merged a PR. There have been no contributions to the master branch since then.

During this period, @broady published a tag in May (as requested in #259). This was the first tag since May 2018. In June, @bep published another tag, after merging #822.

There are new minor fixes that are being accumulated in the list of pending PRs. For example, I was about to merge all of these in a new `trivial` branch: <strike>#887 (+1 −0)</strike>, #896 (+62 −0), #899 (+14 −1), <strike>#912 (+5 −3)</strike>, #929 (+1 −1), #936 (+1 −1), <strike>#944 (+1 −1 )</strike>, <strike>#947 (+3 −6)</strike>, <strike>#948 (+9 −15)</strike>, #949 (+1 −1), <strike>#953 (+104 −9)</strike>, <strike>#954 (+4 −2)</strike>. However, I feel that such a PR might still be open for several weeks before it is reviewed and merged.

Therefore, I'm opening this issue to ask about the maintenance/governance status of this project. I have identified six users with write permissions (mentioned above), but none of them seems to be actively taking the lead. I understand that other priorities arise; hence I'm not asking any of you to step forward. Nonetheless, it is daunting for potential contributors to see PRs which are already implemented and reviewed be laying around for several months. Furthermore, some users are continuously being called, with no response; which must be annoying at some point. I think we should address this as a community.

Moreover, cobra is imported by more than 12k projects (https://godoc.org/github.com/spf13/cobra?importers) and it has >13k stars. It is a very popular project and lots of users are affected by bugs and/or breaking changes. I understand that we need to be careful with pushing changes too fast. Would it be feasible to have a `dev` branch where most of the PRs can be merged faster? It would allow to significantly reduce the number of open PRs, so that *trickier* issues are more visible.

author: knz
title: Flag() docstring is incorrect, also need way to get merged flags before parse
body:
At github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach we have a need to do a few things with command line parsing that would really benefit from a single accessor to the complete flag set, including both local and persistent flags.

Today the doc string for the `(*Command) Flags()` method says "Flags returns the complete FlagSet that applies to this command (local and persistent declared here and by all parents)" but this is incorrect!

Since `Flags()` does not call `mergePersistentFlags()` itself, it only returns the local flags *until mergePersistentFlags() has been called by another method*.

For example, `Flags()` will return the merged set after `Parse()` has been called,  or after `LocalFlags()` has been called. It does not return the merged set if it's the first method to be called.

This means it is hard for user code to rely on `Flags()` to get a merged set. Especially in an `init()` function before `Parse()` has been called.

The proper course of action is:

1. fix the doc string to clarify what the function truly does
2. add another method that gives access to the merged set (e.g. by calling `mergePersistentFlags()` first and then returning the result of `Flags()`).

author: didrocks
title: subcommand handling is inconsistent
body:
This is with cobra v0.0.5.

This is some kind of meta-bug (we can separate this if needed, but I think a general view can help getting a global schema) to gather some of where subcommand support in cobra is falling short. It has a little overlap with bug #870, pr #842, and as I saw the issue discussion that once 1.0 is out, there is some willingness to revisit the maintainance governance, I think this is the right moment to discuss this.

Here is a small example:
foo has 3 subcommands, one having sub subcommand and another one being hidden:
foo:
  - sub1 (alias "alias1")
    - subA
    - subB
  - sub2
  - sub3 (hidden).
    Flag --bar

The base code is:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"

	"github.com/spf13/cobra"
)

var (
	rootCmd = &cobra.Command{
		Use:           "foo",
		SilenceErrors: true,
	}

	subCmd1 = &cobra.Command{
		Use:     "sub1",
		Aliases: []string{"alias1"},
	}

	subCmdA = &cobra.Command{
		Use: "subsubA",
		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}

	subCmdB = &cobra.Command{
		Use: "subsubB",
		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}

	subCmd2 = &cobra.Command{
		Use: "sub2",
		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}

	subCmd3 = &cobra.Command{
		Use:    "sub3",
		Hidden: true,
		Run:    func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}
)

func init() {
	rootCmd.AddCommand(subCmd1, subCmd2, subCmd3)
	subCmd1.AddCommand(subCmdA, subCmdB)
	subCmd3.Flags().Bool("bar", false, "")
}

func main() {
	if err := rootCmd.Execute(); err != nil {
		fmt.Println(err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

# Requiring subcommands

We don't want to be able to run `foo` or `foo sub1` without any arguments, but force providing a subcommand. We could specify `ValidArgs` at this stage, but the error message is then confusing and doesn't mention subcommands. This is easily doable by a dedicated runE:
```go
...
rootCmd = &cobra.Command{
		Use:           "foo",
		SilenceErrors: true,
		RunE:          requireSubcommand,
	}

	subCmd1 = &cobra.Command{
		Use:     "sub1",
		Aliases: []string{"alias1"},
		RunE:    requireSubcommand,
	}
...
func requireSubcommand(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
	return fmt.Errorf("%s requires a subcommand", cmd.Name())
}
...
```

With this:
```
$ ./foo
Usage:
  foo [flags]
  foo [command]

Available Commands:
  help        Help about any command
  sub1        
  sub2        

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for foo

Use "foo [command] --help" for more information about a command.

foo requires a subcommand
$ ./foo sub1
Usage:
  foo sub1 [flags]
  foo sub1 [command]

Aliases:
  sub1, alias1

Available Commands:
  subsubA     
  subsubB     

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for sub1

Use "foo sub1 [command] --help" for more information about a command.

sub1 requires a subcommand
```

Only sub1 and sub2 are shown, as expected, in addition to help.

## Changing usage
Note though that the usage isn't correct:

```
  foo [flags]
  foo [command]
```

So, we change this to:

```go
Use:           "foo COMMAND",
...
Use:     "sub1 COMMAND",
...
```

Now, the usage is a little bit better, but still not accurate:

```
Usage:
  foo sub1 COMMAND [flags]
  foo sub1 [command]
```

I couldn't find in cobra's code any exported function which enables removing the invalid "foo sub1 [command]" line.

I think in general a revisited way to tell "this command requires subcommands only" would help fixing the additional code and other issues.

# Suggestions for command

Suggestions for subcommands works, just after the root command:
```
$ ./foo s
unknown command "s" for "foo"

Did you mean this?
        sub1
        sub2
```

cobra only shows non hidden matching commands and not the alias, great.

## Help (which is a valid subcommand of the rootCmd isn't suggested)
```
$ ./foo h
unknown command "h" for "foo"
```

## Alias are not suggested either
Similar, aliases are not suggested even if it should match:
```
$ ./foo a
unknown command "a" for "foo"
```

## Sub-subcommand's suggestion doesn't work

Subcommands of sub1 doesn't show up any suggestions:
```
$ ./foo sub1 s
Usage:
  foo sub1 COMMAND [flags]
  foo sub1 [command]

Aliases:
  sub1, alias1

Available Commands:
  subsubA     
  subsubB     

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for sub1

Use "foo sub1 [command] --help" for more information about a command.

sub1 requires a subcommand
```

We can see that:
- runE was called (hence the error "sub1 requires a subcommand")
- no suggestion was provided. This is due to `legacyArgs()`` not being called as `commandFound.Args != nil` for subcommand (in `Find()`). This is the only place where the internal `cmd.findSuggestions()` is called (with valid args checking, more on that later).
Even if `legacyArgs()` would have been called, the check `!cmd.HasParent()` would prevent it to give any suggestions.

I would prefer to not have to duplicate the strings and checks for the internal `findSuggestions()` (see the comment on the first bug report as well, where we have duplicated string).I found a way to mitigate this and the previous issues is to use `Args: cobra.OnlyValidArgs,` and expand `ValidArgs` dynamically.

```go
...
	subCmd1 = &cobra.Command{
		Use:     "sub1 COMMAND",
		Aliases: []string{"alias1"},
		RunE:    requireSubcommand,
		Args: cobra.OnlyValidArgs,
	}
...
func init() {
        ...
	addSubcommandsToValidArgs(subCmd1)
}

func addSubcommandsToValidArgs(cmd *cobra.Command) {
	validArgs := cmd.ValidArgs
	for _, c := range cmd.Commands() {
		validArgs = append(validArgs, c.Name())
	}
	cmd.ValidArgs = validArgs
}
...
```

We now have subcommands suggestions:
```
$ ./foo sub1 s
Usage:
  foo sub1 COMMAND [flags]
  foo sub1 [command]

Aliases:
  sub1, alias1

Available Commands:
  subsubA     
  subsubB     

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for sub1

Use "foo sub1 [command] --help" for more information about a command.

invalid argument "s" for "foo sub1"

Did you mean this?
        subsubA
        subsubB
```

However, the experience vastly different from the one printing on the root cmd:
```
$ ./foo s
unknown command "s" for "foo"

Did you mean this?
        sub1
        sub2
```
-> this is way shorter (no usage printed), and we have "unkown command…" instead of "invalid argument".

If we add similarly the same kind of argument check on the root command, of course, the inconsistency is "fixed", but this is by using the less accurate version, the desired strings being in `legacyArgs()`.

Note that this doesn't work though for aliases or "help" command, even if they are added and attached to the root command:
```go
...
func addSubcommandsToValidArgs(cmd *cobra.Command) {
	validArgs := cmd.ValidArgs

	// Add subcommands and aliases
	for _, c := range cmd.Commands() {
		validArgs = append(validArgs, c.Name())
		validArgs = append(validArgs, c.Aliases...)
	}

	// Add help for root command
	if !cmd.HasParent() {
		fmt.Println("ooo")
		validArgs = append(validArgs, "help")
	}

	cmd.ValidArgs = validArgs
}
...
+ for rootCmd:
Args:          cobra.OnlyValidArgs,
and call to addSubcommandsToValidArgs(rootCmd)
```

This returns:
```
$ ./foo h
Usage:
  foo COMMAND [flags]
  foo [command]

Available Commands:
  help        Help about any command
  sub1        
  sub2        

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for foo

Use "foo [command] --help" for more information about a command.

invalid argument "h" for "foo"
```

And aliases don't work either:
```
$ ./foo a
Usage:
  foo COMMAND [flags]
  foo [command]

Available Commands:
  help        Help about any command
  sub1        
  sub2        

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for foo

Use "foo [command] --help" for more information about a command.

invalid argument "a" for "foo"
```

This is due to `SuggestionsFor()` only checking subcommands (so discaring "help") and their names (discaring thus `Aliases`).
Note that we could potentially override it from the program and attach a new function to each command, as it's exported, it will need to replace c.commands by c.Commands().

## No suggestion for flags:

There is no suggestion for flags:
```
$ ./foo sub3 --b
ooo
Usage:
  foo sub3 [flags]

Flags:
      --bar    
  -h, --help   help for sub3

unknown flag: --b
```

"--bar" could be suggested. This is what the initial bug reported I linked at was about.

# completions once entered in a "hidden" command 

Completions for subcommands are also generally puzzled by this.
Note that to not puzzle the result with hidden commands, I needed to remove 
```go
addSubcommandsToValidArgs(rootCmd)
```
As other "help", "aliases" and hidden commands would show up (which is one of the limitation of the previous approach).

Via a call to `rootCmd.GenBashCompletionFile` and sourcing the resulting file, here is what we get:
```
$ foo sub[tab][tab]
sub1  sub2  
```
-> sub3 is hidden, as expected.

## Aliases and help
However, Aliases, nor Help aren't completed `$ foo [tab]` completes to "foo sub".

## Hidden command completion
Worse, hidden commands, once typed, doesn't complete and provide invalid completions:
```
$ foo sub3 [tab]
-> completes to $ foo sub3 sub[tab][tab]
sub1  sub2 
```

From a user perspective, I would expect not being completed by other commands, but by available flags on sub3 (as I typed the "hidden command" already).

Sorry for all this to be a little bit long to digest, but I wanted to put everything where I think cobra is falling short in term of subcommand handling vs suggestions and completions. I dont' like to open meta-bug, but I guess putting all those issues in perspective in a single place help if there is a desire to rework that part. Am I wrong on my approach and things can be mitigate in a more consistant way?

# For reference, complete code

This is the one with some workarounds as previously stated (but doesn't fix all the issues as mentionned above)


```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"

	"github.com/spf13/cobra"
)

var (
	rootCmd = &cobra.Command{
		Use:           "foo COMMAND",
		SilenceErrors: true,
		RunE:          requireSubcommand,
		Args:          cobra.OnlyValidArgs,
	}

	subCmd1 = &cobra.Command{
		Use:     "sub1 COMMAND",
		Aliases: []string{"alias1"},
		RunE:    requireSubcommand,
		Args:    cobra.OnlyValidArgs,
	}

	subCmdA = &cobra.Command{
		Use: "subsubA",
		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}

	subCmdB = &cobra.Command{
		Use: "subsubB",
		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}

	subCmd2 = &cobra.Command{
		Use: "sub2",
		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}

	subCmd3 = &cobra.Command{
		Use:    "sub3",
		Hidden: true,
		Run:    func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {},
	}
)

func init() {
	rootCmd.AddCommand(subCmd1, subCmd2, subCmd3)
	subCmd1.AddCommand(subCmdA, subCmdB)
	subCmd3.Flags().Bool("bar", false, "")
        // disabled for shell completion examples
	//addSubcommandsToValidArgs(rootCmd)
	addSubcommandsToValidArgs(subCmd1)
}

func requireSubcommand(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
	return fmt.Errorf("%s requires a subcommand", cmd.Name())
}

func addSubcommandsToValidArgs(cmd *cobra.Command) {
	validArgs := cmd.ValidArgs

	// Add subcommands and aliases
	for _, c := range cmd.Commands() {
		validArgs = append(validArgs, c.Name())
		validArgs = append(validArgs, c.Aliases...)
	}

	// Add help for root command
	if !cmd.HasParent() {
		validArgs = append(validArgs, "help")
	}

	cmd.ValidArgs = validArgs
}

func main() {
	if err := rootCmd.Execute(); err != nil {
		fmt.Println(err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

In summary, the remaining issues are:
- no "help" command suggestion
- no alias suggestion
- no flag suggestion
- incorrect completion when starting completing hidden command "sub3"

author: johnaoss
title: docs: Centralize documentation
body:
As the Wiki feature is enabled on this repo, I suggest that we move the docs to a central location.

## Where
Ideally this could be the Wiki. We could copy over all of the `.md` files into there with minimal effort. As a temporary measure, we can keep both the `.md` files in-repo, and just mirror them in the Wiki as separate pages, with the end goal of removing from the repo entirely. 

If the Wiki is deemed as an improper place to put this documentation, I then suggest something like a `/docs` folder. This is seemingly common in several other Go projects, and would allow the documentation to still be kept locally after cloning the repo. The only downside for this is that there currently exists a `/doc` folder, which *could* be confusing to some. 

## Why 

This would have the benefit of allowing a place for more in-depth tutorials for people looking to adapt `cobra` for their own use cases. This could also contain a sort of FAQ for common issues. 
As an additional benefit, this could potentially provide a single place to address the concerns @umarcor outlined in issue #959. 

The main reason I'm asking for something like this is that there seem to be a couple open issues about documentation that are unresolved. I am planning to contribute fixes to those issues, I'm just unsure of where to place said docs. I personally think the Wiki could be a good place for me to start, unless there is some other method that is preferred.

I suggest reopening https://github.com/spf13/cobra/pull/887, at least for me it works fine.

author: marckhouzam
title: Possible breaking change: help now goes to STDERR
body:
As part of #922 the help message was recently changed from being printed to STDOUT to now being printed to STDERR. 

This sounds like a breaking change.  Some scripts could be written with the expectation that the help message is on stdout, and changing it would break such scripts.  I know the change broke one of Helm's acceptance testing scripts (https://github.com/helm/acceptance-testing/pull/64).  We've discussed this at the Helm developper call and we felt it was worth bringing up to the Cobra project.

Doing a little digging I found that sending the help message to STDOUT was a conscious decision done in #303, 3 years ago.  Changing back to STDERR however seemed more of a "why not" decision, as can be interpreted from the original code change text from https://github.com/spf13/cobra/pull/642#issue-171823645 from which #922 was based, which states:
> Usage output in this scenario is also now sent to stderr instead of stdout, which is better for scripting and seems more consistent with surrounding code.

(Note that although the text says "Usage output" it is actually the Help output that was changed.)

The specific change in question is not part of a COBRA release yet so could easily be reverted to have the help message be sent to STDOUT again and avoid breaking automation scripts.

I can provide a PR if there is agreement to revert.

Thank you.

/cc @bruceadowns @bogem

author: rochaporto
title: go test failing with custom flags
body:
With tests relying on golden files managed by an update flag:
```
var update = flag.Bool("update", false, "update golden test data")
...
go test -v ./... -update
```

With Go 1.13, a project relying on cobra and using the pattern above ends up seeing:
```
go test -v -run . ./... -update
flag provided but not defined: -update
```
I believe this is due to https://github.com/golang/go/issues/31859 which refers to https://github.com/golang/go/commit/fbc6a972226f889d2ab1150468755615098ee80f as the breaking change.

author: kurtpeek
title: Cobra picking up a flag default value from a different command?
body:
This test Cobra app, https://github.com/kurtpeek/myCobraApp, illustrates the issue. It was scaffolded using the Cobra generator with the following commands:

```
cobra add serve
cobra add config
cobra add command
cobra add install -p 'commandCmd'
cobra add erase -p 'commandCmd'
```
In `config.go`, a string variable called `deviceUUID` is declared and bound to a flag using with a default value of `"1234"`, similar to the following:

```go
var deviceUUID string

// configCmd represents the config command
var configCmd = &cobra.Command{
}

func init() {
	rootCmd.AddCommand(configCmd)

	configCmd.Flags().StringVar(&deviceUUID, "deviceUUID", "1234", "Device UUID")
}
```

Similarly in `serve.go`, the same variable is given a default value of "5678":

```go
// serveCmd represents the serve command
var serveCmd = &cobra.Command{
	Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
		fmt.Println("deviceUUID:", deviceUUID)
		fmt.Println("serve called")
	},
}

func init() {
	rootCmd.AddCommand(serveCmd)

	serveCmd.Flags().StringVar(&deviceUUID, "deviceUUID", "5678", "Device UUID")
}
```
Finally, in `erase.go`, the default value for the flag is set to `"0000"`:

```go
	eraseCmd.Flags().StringVar(&deviceUUID, "deviceUUID", "0000", "Device UUID")
```

When I run the `erase` command, I get that the `deviceUUID` is the default one defined in `serve.go`:

```
> go run main.go command erase
deviceUUID: 5678
erase called
```

Why is it picking up the default value from a different command? The scaffolding code comment

> Cobra supports local flags which will only run when this command is called directly

would suggest that the local flags should only run when each command is called directly?

body:
I'm writing a library wrapper around cobra for [discordgo](https://github.com/bwmarrin/discordgo).

The library works by invoking a user provided command factory that needs to return a root command.

The problem I'm running into is that when a user invokes a command using something like !test, and "test" is not a valid subcommand, cobra outputs `Error: unknown command "test" for "!"`.  
While this is intended behaviour, discord bot best practices state that invalid commands should not be output due to possible conflicts:  
https://github.com/meew0/discord-bot-best-practices (Rule 6)

This is only an issue because the root command use is the bot prefix (so `!`, for example). On unix, the root command would be unique (since it's the name of the binary), but on discord, multiple bots can share the same prefix.

My current approach looks something like this 
```go
if !root.IsAvailableCommand() && !root.IsAdditionalHelpTopicCommand() {
  // error function with ErrInvalidCommand
  return
}
```
before invoking the command.

This is rather cumbersome and hard to understand, and I am not certain it will catch every use case.

Is there a cleaner way to solve this problem?

Source code is here: https://github.com/cfi2017/dgcobra

author: brianpursley
title: Feature request to support multi-word usage for root command
body:
Currently, cobra assumes that the command to display for usage in help is the first word.  However, sometimes the root command can actually be multiple words.  This is the case for kubectl plugins for example.

There is a [related issue opened in the krew repository](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/krew/issues/521) and it was proposed that the preferred fix may actually be to see if cobra can be changed to show the entire value of `Use` for the root command and not just the first word.

---

Here is an example illustrating the problem:

Consider this simple cobra application, **main.go**.  Imagine that this code implements a kubectl plugin called myplugin:
```
package main

import (
	"github.com/spf13/cobra"
)

func main() {
	var rootCmd = &cobra.Command{
		Use: "kubectl myplugin",
	}

	rootCmd.AddCommand(&cobra.Command{
		Use: "dosomething",
		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
		},
	})

	_ = rootCmd.Execute()
}
```


**PROBLEM 1:** When you run it and the default help is displayed, it says the usage is just `kubectl`.  But the code above says it should be `kubectl myplugin`.
```
go run main.go
```

```
Usage:
  kubectl [command]

Available Commands:
  dosomething 
  help        Help about any command

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for kubectl

Use "kubectl [command] --help" for more information about a command.
```


**PROBLEM 2:** When you run help for a specific subcommand, it similarly only shows the first word of the command:
```
go run main.go dosomething --help
```

```
Usage:
  kubectl dosomething [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for dosomething
```

---

I'm looking for any thoughts and ideas on this problem.  

I was thinking about trying to make a PR that would support something like this, but I don't want to do anything that would break existing apps. 

One idea would be to allow "escaping" spaces in the Use property.

I'm looking specifically at this function in command.go:
```
func (c *Command) Name() string {
	name := c.Use
	i := strings.Index(name, " ")
	if i >= 0 {
		name = name[:i]
	}
	return name
}
```

Instead of looking for the first space, can we change this so that I can specify something like `kubectl\ myplugin` and it will not consider `\ ` to be a space in this case because it is escaped, but it would still render as a space (without the `\`) in help output.

author: marckhouzam
title: Go completion broken when MarkPersistentRequiredFlag() called on root command
body:
While working on supporting required flags for Go completions (Fish and Zsh v2) I hit the following bug.

If a persistent flag on the root command is marked as required, e.g., 
```
rootCmd.PersistentFlags().String("flag", "", "required persistent")
rootCmd.MarkPersistentFlagRequired("flag")
```
it breaks the `__complete` command.

This is because the `__complete` command, being a child of the root command, inherits the required persistent flag, and since that flag is not specified when calling `__complete`, the `__complete` command fails to execute.
```
$ ./testprog __complete ""
Error: required flag(s) "flag" not set
```
I think it is and unlikely case though; if the root command would have a required persistent flag, it would imply that that flag would need to be specified in every single case of calling the program; I have trouble imagining a use case for that.

Still, it should probably be fixed.
I don't have a solution right now, but I will be investigating if defining a `PreRun` on `__complete`  can allow us to turn off required flags for `__complete`.

In the unlikely case of this bug, the impacts are:
- bash: Go custom completions (`ValidArgsFunction` and `RegisterFlagCompletionFunc()`) would not work (but everything else would)
- fish: all completions would not work

author: wfernandes
title: cobra init cmd documentation seems to be incorrrect
body:
As I was playing around with `cobra init` I noticed the help documentation seems to be at odds with the [cobra/README](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/11ba63fc3bc37818c471fc7912783e6909da4645/cobra/README.md#cobra-init) documentation.

The `cobra init --help` prints out the following:
```
  * If a name is provided, it will be created in the current directory;
  * If no name is provided, the current directory will be assumed;
  * If a relative path is provided, it will be created inside $GOPATH
    (e.g. github.com/spf13/hugo);
  * If an absolute path is provided, it will be created;
  * If the directory already exists but is empty, it will be used.

Init will not use an existing directory with contents.
```

However, as I was using the command and reading through the documentation, the following statements seem to be incorrect. 
```
  * If a relative path is provided, it will be created inside $GOPATH
    (e.g. github.com/spf13/hugo);
  * If an absolute path is provided, it will be created;

Init will not use an existing directory with contents.
```

Upon inspection of the code, we seem to be prepending the current working directory to the argument passed in. 
https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/11ba63fc3bc37818c471fc7912783e6909da4645/cobra/cmd/init.go#L46-L58

So I guess the question here is: **what is the expected behavior? Is to initialize a project in the current working directory? Or should we be supporting relative paths in GOPATH and absolute paths?**

title: Square brackets in the description causes problems with zsh
body:
I think I found a bug with zsh completion in cobra 1.0.0: If I put square brackets in a command description they do not get escaped correctly causing problems. 
[Here](https://github.com/arduino/arduino-cli/blob/6061cbf6dab73f6386c6e6f333a8c145d08315ce/cli/cli.go#L90) there's an example of the line causing problems.
I "patched" this behaviour with:
```
buf := new(bytes.Buffer)
	cmd.Root().GenZshCompletion(buf)
	r := strings.NewReplacer("[", "\\[", "]", "\\]") //insert escaping before [ and ]
	s := r.Replace(buf.String())
	s = strings.ReplaceAll(s, "\\[1\\]", "[1]") // revert the case
	os.Stdout.WriteString(s)
```
I think this will be fixed in https://github.com/spf13/cobra/pull/1070 but I'm opening that just for reference
